title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 160 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 783–785 (Night 160, continuing directly from nights-159), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 160 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The slave-girl speaks with ʿAlī in private and leaves, and the jeweller who sat with him, a friend of the absent Abū al-Ḥasan, tells ʿAlī he must have dealings with the caliph's palace: he knows the girl as Shams al-Nahār's maid, who once brought him an order for a necklace. ʿAlī, shaken, tells him the whole story; the jeweller offers to keep him company in Abū al-Ḥasan's place, and ʿAlī answers with two lines of verse. Then ʿAlī tells him what the girl came to say — that she believes ʿAlī himself had Abū al-Ḥasan sent away to Basra as a ruse to end the letters and meetings, and that she would not believe his oath — and the jeweller swears to find a way to her without exposing anyone. ʿAlī begs him to keep the secret and weeps as he goes. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلسِّتِّينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-sittīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing for-the-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixtieth night,
sentences.n: A new way of counting: al-mūfiya, “the one completing”, is the feminine active participle of Form IV awfā, “to fulfil, bring to full measure”, and li-, “for”, names the number it completes. So “the night completing the sixty after the hundred” is the hundred and sixtieth. Round tens are counted this way in the night-headings, since sittūn, “sixty”, has no ordinal of its own. The alif of المائة is not pronounced: the word is miʾa, and its hamza is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ لَمَّا دَخَلَتْ عَلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ تَقَدَّمَتْ عِنْدَهُ وَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَتَحَدَّثَتْ مَعَهُ سِرًّا وَهُوَ يُقْسِمُ فِي أَثْنَاءِ الْكَلَامِ وَيَحْلِفُ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَتَكَلَّمْ بِذَلِكَ ثُمَّ وَدَّعَتْهُ وَمَضَتْ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jāriyata lammā dakhalat ʿalā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin taqaddamat ʿindahu wa-sallamat ʿalayhi wa-taḥaddathat maʿahu sirran wa-huwa yuqsimu fī athnāʾi al-kalāmi wa-yaḥlifu annahu lam yatakallam bi-dhālika thumma waddaʿathu wa-maḍat
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the slave-girl, when she entered upon ʿAlī son of Bakkār, came-forward to-him and greeted him and talked with-him secretly, and he swears in the course of the talk and takes-oath that he did-not speak of that; then she bade-him-farewell and went.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the slave-girl came in to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār she stepped up to him, greeted him, and spoke with him privately; and all the while he was swearing and vowing that he had not breathed a word of it. Then she took her leave and went.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up where Night 159 broke off, repeating its last words (taqaddamat ʿindahu wa-sallamat ʿalayhi). dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” someone, the verb choosing ʿalā. sirran, “in secret”, is an adverbial accusative. wa-huwa yuqsimu …, “while he swears …”: a circumstantial clause, its present tense describing what went on during the talk. yuqsimu (Form IV aqsama) and yaḥlifu both mean “to swear”, doubled for emphasis. takallama bi-, “to speak of, let out”: bi- marks what is spoken. What ʿAlī denies is not spelled out; the sense is that he has told no one of the affair.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الرَّجُلُ صَاحِبُ أَبِى الْحَسَنِ جَوْهَرِيًّا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-rajulu ṣāḥibu Abī al-Ḥasani jawhariyyan
sentences.l: And the man, the companion of Abū al-Ḥasan, was a jeweller.
sentences.i: Now the man, Abū al-Ḥasan's friend, was a jeweller.
sentences.n: al-rajul, “the man”, is the friend who was sitting with ʿAlī; ṣāḥibu Abī al-Ḥasan stands beside it in apposition, and jawhariyyan, “a jeweller”, is the accusative predicate of kāna. The print writes Abī here with ى (ابى); elsewhere in this night it has ابي. jawharī is formed from jawhar, “jewel, gem”, with the -ī of trade or origin.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا انْصَرَفَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَجَدَ لِلْكَلَامِ مَحَلًّا فَقَالَ لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ لَاشَكَّ وَلَارَيْبَ أَنَّ لِدَارِ الْخِلَافَةِ عَلَيْكَ مُطَالَبَةً أَوْ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهَا مُعَامَلَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā inṣarafati al-jāriyatu wajada li-al-kalāmi maḥallan fa-qāla li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin lā shakka wa-lā rayba anna li-dāri al-khilāfati ʿalayka muṭālabatan aw baynaka wa-baynahā muʿāmalatan
sentences.l: And when the slave-girl departed, he-found for-the-speaking a place, and he-said to-ʿAlī son of Bakkār: No doubt and no uncertainty that the House of the Caliphate has against-you a claim, or between-you and-between-it (there is) a dealing.
sentences.i: When the slave-girl had gone, he found his opening to speak, and said to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, “There is no doubt about it, none at all: either the palace of the caliph has some claim on you, or there are dealings between you and it.”
sentences.n: The print has الجاربة, a misprint for الجارية, corrected here. wajada li-al-kalāmi maḥallan, “he found a place for speaking”: li- says what the room was for; he had waited for the girl to leave. The print runs lā and its noun together twice (لاشك ولاريب); the spacing is kept. lā shakka and lā rayba, “no doubt”, take the accusative without tanwīn, the lā that denies a whole class. dār al-khilāfa, “the House of the Caliphate”, is the caliph's palace, where Shams al-Nahār lives. In li-dāri … ʿalayka muṭālaba, li- marks the one who has the claim and ʿalā the one it lies on: “the palace has a claim against you”. muṭālaba, “demand, claim”, and muʿāmala, “dealing, business”, are accusative after anna, their predicates coming first; the two rhyme.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَمَنْ أَعْلَمَكَ بِذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-man aʿlamaka bi-dhālika
sentences.l: And he-said: And who informed-you of that?
sentences.i: ʿAlī said, “And who told you that?”
sentences.n: aʿlama, “to inform” (Form IV of ʿalima), takes the person as object and bi- for the thing made known. wa-, “and”, at the head of a question is a sharp rejoinder.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ مَعْرِفَتِي بِهَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةِ لِأَنَّهَا جَارِيَةُ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَكَانَتْ جَاءَتْنِي مِنْ مُدَّةٍ بِرُقْعَةٍ مَكْتُوبٍ فِيهَا أَنَّهَا تَشْتَهِي عِقْدَ جَوْهَرٍ فَأَرْسَلْتُ إِلَيْهَا عِقْدًا ثَمِينًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla maʿrifatī bi-hādhihi al-jāriyati li-annahā jāriyatu Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-kānat jāʾatnī min muddatin bi-ruqʿatin maktūbin fīhā annahā tashtahī ʿiqda jawharin fa-arsaltu ilayhā ʿiqdan thamīnan
sentences.l: And he-said: My-knowledge of this slave-girl, because she (is) the slave-girl of Shams al-Nahār; and she had come-to-me some time ago with a note written in-it that she desires a necklace of jewels, and I-sent to-her a precious necklace.
sentences.i: He said, “I know this girl: she is Shams al-Nahār's maid. Some time ago she came to me with a note saying that her mistress wanted a jewelled necklace, and I sent her a costly one.”
sentences.n: maʿrifatī bi-…, “my acquaintance with …”: ʿarafa and maʿrifa take bi- for the person known. The answer is a bare noun, “(what told me is) my knowing this girl”. kānat jāʾatnī, “she had come to me”: kāna with a perfect gives a pluperfect. jāʾa bi-, “to come with, bring”: bi- marks what she brought. min muddatin, “some while since”. maktūbin fīhā, “written in it”, is impersonal, so the participle stays masculine though ruqʿa, “note, slip of paper”, is feminine. annahā tashtahī, “that she desires”: the “she” is Shams al-Nahār. The hamza of جاءتني is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ كَلَامَهُ اضْطَرَبَ حَتَّى خُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ التَّلَفُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin kalāmahu iḍṭaraba ḥattā khushiya ʿalayhi al-talafu
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār heard his-speech, he-was-agitated until the perishing was-feared for-him.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār heard what he said, he was so shaken that they feared for his life.
sentences.n: iḍṭaraba, “to be thrown into confusion, tremble” (Form VIII of ḍaraba). khushiya ʿalayhi al-talafu, “ruin was feared for him”: the passive of khashiya, with ʿalā for the person feared for. talaf is destruction, here death.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَاجَعَ نَفْسَهُ وَقَالَ يَا أَخِي سَأَلْتُكَ بِاللَّهِ مِنْ أَيْنَ تَعْرِفُهَا
sentences.tr: thumma rājaʿa nafsahu wa-qāla yā akhī saʾaltuka bi-Allāhi min ayna taʿrifuhā
sentences.l: Then he-returned-to himself and said: O my-brother, I-ask-you by God, from where do-you-know-her?
sentences.i: Then he collected himself and said, “My brother, I beg you by God, how do you know her?”
sentences.n: rājaʿa nafsahu, “he went back to himself”, is to recover one's composure. saʾaltuka bi-Allāhi, “I have asked you by God”: the perfect is used for an entreaty made in the act of speaking, and bi- is the bi- of oath. The hamza of سألتك is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ دَعِ الْإِلْحَاحَ فِى السُّؤَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-jawhariyyu daʿi al-ilḥāḥa fī al-suʾāli
sentences.l: And the jeweller said to-him: Leave the insisting in the questioning.
sentences.i: The jeweller said to him, “Do not press me so with questions.”
sentences.n: daʿ, “leave, let be”, is the imperative of the verb whose present is yadaʿu; it takes a kasra before the article. ilḥāḥ, “insistence, importunity” (verbal noun of Form IV alaḥḥa). The print writes fī as فى; the hamza of السؤال is its own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ لَا أَرْجِعُ عَنْكَ إِلَّا إِذَا أَخْبَرْتَنِي بِالصَّحِيحِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin lā arjiʿu ʿanka illā idhā akhbartanī bi-al-ṣaḥīḥi
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said to-him: I-will-not turn-back from-you except if you-tell-me the truth.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to him, “I will not let you be unless you tell me the truth.”
sentences.n: rajaʿa ʿan, “to turn back from, give up”: “I will not leave off from you”. akhbara bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the verb chooses bi- for what is told. al-ṣaḥīḥ, “the sound, the true”: the plain truth.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ أَنَا أُخْبِرُكَ بِحَيْثُ لَا يَدْخُلُكَ مِنِّي وَهْمٌ وَلَا يَعْتَرِيكَ مِنْ كَلَامِي انْقِبَاضٌ وَلَا أُخْفِي عَنْكَ سِرًّا وَأُبَيِّنُ لَكَ حَقِيقَةَ الْأَمْرِ وَلَكِنْ بِشَرْطِ أَنْ تُخْبِرَنِي بِحَقِيقَةِ حَالِكَ وَسَبَبِ مَرَضِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-jawhariyyu anā ukhbiruka bi-ḥaythu lā yadkhuluka minnī wahmun wa-lā yaʿtarīka min kalāmī inqibāḍun wa-lā ukhfī ʿanka sirran wa-ubayyinu laka ḥaqīqata al-amri wa-lākin bi-sharṭi an tukhbiranī bi-ḥaqīqati ḥālika wa-sababi maraḍika
sentences.l: And the jeweller said to-him: I tell-you in-such-a-way-that there-does-not-enter-you from-me misgiving, and there-does-not-come-upon-you from my-speech a-shrinking, and I-do-not hide from-you a secret, and I-make-clear to-you the truth of the matter; but on condition that you-tell-me the truth of your-state and the cause of your-sickness.
sentences.i: The jeweller said to him, “I will tell you, and in such a way that no suspicion of me will cross your mind and nothing I say will trouble you. I will keep no secret from you and will lay the whole matter bare; but only on condition that you tell me the truth about yourself and the cause of your sickness.”
sentences.n: bi-ḥaythu, “in such a way that”: ḥaythu, “where”, after bi- introduces a result. wahm is a notion that crosses the mind, here suspicion; inqibāḍ (Form VII, compare inqabaḍa in Night 159) a shrinking of the heart, unease. yaʿtarī, “to befall, come over” (Form VIII). bi-sharṭi an, “on condition that”: bi- here is “on, under”. tukhbiranī is subjunctive after an.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَهُ بِخَبَرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarahu bi-khabarihi
sentences.l: And he-informed-him of his-story.
sentences.i: So ʿAlī told him his story.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-khabarihi, “he told him his tale”: verb and noun from the same root, a common figure. bi- marks what is told.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ وَاللَّهِ يَا أَخِي مَا حَمَلَنِي عَلَى كِتْمَانِ أَمْرِي عَنْ غَيْرِكَ إِلَّا مَخَافَةُ أَنَّ النَّاسَ تَكْشِفُ أَسْتَارَ بَعْضِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla wa-Allāhi yā akhī mā ḥamalanī ʿalā kitmāni amrī ʿan ghayrika illā makhāfatu anna al-nāsa takshifu astāra baʿḍihā
sentences.l: Then he-said: By God, O my-brother, nothing carried-me to concealing my-affair from others-than-you except fear that people uncover the veils of one-another.
sentences.i: Then he said, “By God, my brother, nothing made me hide my affair from anyone but you except the fear that people tear away each other's veils.”
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: the wa- of oath. ḥamala ʿalā, “to drive (someone) to”: the verb chooses ʿalā. mā … illā, “nothing … except”, puts the stress on makhāfa, “fear”, which is the subject. ʿan ghayrika, “from other than you”: from everyone but the man he is now confiding in. al-nās, “people”, is treated as a feminine singular, with takshifu and baʿḍihā; kashf al-astār, “lifting the veils”, is exposing another's secrets.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَأَنَا مَا أَرَدْتُ اجْتِمَاعِي بِكَ إِلَّا لِشِدَّةِ مَحَبَّتِي لَكَ وَغَيْرَتِي فِي كُلِّ حَالٍ عَلَيْكَ وَشَفَقَتِي عَلَى قَلْبِكَ مِنْ أَلَمِ الْفِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-jawhariyyu li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-anā mā aradtu ijtimāʿī bika illā li-shiddati maḥabbatī laka wa-ghayratī fī kulli ḥālin ʿalayka wa-shafaqatī ʿalā qalbika min alami al-firāqi
sentences.l: And the jeweller said to-ʿAlī son of Bakkār: And I did-not want my-meeting with-you except for-the-strength of my-love for-you, and my-jealous-care in every state for-you, and my-pity for your-heart from the pain of the parting.
sentences.i: The jeweller said to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, “And I sought your company for no other reason than my great affection for you, my zeal for you in every case, and my pity for your heart in the pain of separation.
sentences.n: ijtimāʿī bika, “my meeting with you”: ijtamaʿa takes bi- for the person met. li-shiddati, “because of the strength of”: li- gives the reason. ghayra ʿalā is the protective jealousy one feels for someone dear; shafaqa ʿalā, “compassion, anxious care for”: both nouns choose ʿalā.

sentences.t: عَسَي أَكُونُ لَكَ مُؤْنِسًا نِيَابَةً عَنْ صَدِيقِي أَبِي الْحَسَنِ فِي طُولِ غَيْبَتِهِ فَطِبْ نَفْسًا وَقَرَّ عَيْنًا
sentences.tr: ʿasā akūnu laka muʾnisan niyābatan ʿan ṣadīqī Abī al-Ḥasani fī ṭūli ghaybatihi fa-ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan
sentences.l: Perhaps I-shall-be for-you a companion, in-place of my-friend Abū al-Ḥasan in the length of his-absence. So be-good of soul and be-cool of eye.
sentences.i: “Perhaps I may keep you company in place of my friend Abū al-Ḥasan for as long as he is away. So take heart, and be comforted.”
sentences.n: ʿasā, “perhaps, it may be”, is spelt with a final ي (عسي), the print's habit; it is pointed عَسَي and read ʿasā. Here it is followed directly by akūnu, without the an Classical Arabic expects, a Middle Arabic feature. muʾnis, “one who cheers loneliness”, from uns, “intimacy”; its hamza is the print's own. niyābatan ʿan, “as a deputy for”, accusative of manner. Here the print writes Abī with ي. ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan, “be good of soul and cool of eye”: the accusatives say in what respect, and a “cool eye” is the Arabic for contentment, a hot one for tears. qarra is the imperative of the doubled verb; the shadda is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَشَكَرَهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-shakarahu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin ʿalā dhālika wa-anshada hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār thanked-him for that and recited these two verses:
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār thanked him for this and recited these two verses:
sentences.n: shakara … ʿalā, “to thank (someone) for”: the verb chooses ʿalā. hādhayni al-baytayni, “these two verses”, is dual and accusative.

sentences.t:
وَلَوْ قُلْتُ اِنِّيْ صَابِرٌ بَعْدَ بُعْدِهِ * لَكَذَّبَنِيْ دَمْعِيْ وَفَرْطُ نَحِيْبِيْ
وَكَيْفَ اُدَارِيْ مَدْمَعًا جَرَيَانُهُ * عَلَى صَحْنِ خَدِّيْ مِنْ فِرَاقِ حَبِيْبِيْ
sentences.tr:
wa-law qultu innī ṣābirun baʿda buʿdihi * la-kadhdhabanī damʿī wa-farṭu naḥībī
wa-kayfa udārī madmaʿan jarayānuhu * ʿalā ṣaḥni khaddī min firāqi ḥabībī
sentences.l:
And if I-said: I (am) patient after his-going-far, * my-tears and the excess of my-wailing would-give-me-the-lie;
and how shall-I-dissemble a tear-flow whose-running * (is) upon the expanse of my-cheek from the parting of my-beloved?
sentences.i:
Were I to say that I am patient now that he is far away, my tears and my unending sobs would call me a liar;
and how can I hide a flood of tears that runs down my cheek because my beloved is gone?
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اِنِّيْ and اُدَارِيْ, where the edition marks no hamza, and the sukūn it sets on long vowels (اِنِّيْ, نَحِيْبِيْ, حَبِيْبِيْ). baʿda buʿdihi, “after his distance”, plays on two words of one root. law … la-kadhdhabanī: law, “if”, with the perfect for an unreal condition, and la- opening the answer. kadhdhaba (Form II), “to call a liar, give the lie to”. udārī, “I conceal, dissemble” (Form III dārā). madmaʿ is where tears flow, here the flow itself; ṣaḥn al-khadd, “the plain of the cheek”. The beloved is spoken of as “he”, as love poetry customarily does, though the one longed for is Shams al-Nahār.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ سَكَتَ سَاعَةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ قَالَ لِلْجَوْهَرِيِّ أَتَدْرِي مَا سَٰرَّتْنِي بِهِ الْجَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin sakata sāʿatan mina al-zamāni wa-baʿda dhālika qāla li-al-jawhariyyi a-tadrī mā sārratnī bihi al-jāriyatu
sentences.l: Then ʿAlī son of Bakkār was-silent an-hour of time, and after that he-said to-the-jeweller: Do-you-know what the slave-girl confided-to-me (of-it)?
sentences.i: Then ʿAlī ibn Bakkār was silent for a while, and after that he said to the jeweller, “Do you know what the girl told me in confidence?”
sentences.n: thumma inna again opens a new step, so ʿAliyya is accusative; this time the print writes علي with no alif of -an. sāʿatan mina al-zamān, “an hour of time”, is simply “a while”. a-tadrī, “do you know?”: a- is the question prefix. The print has سرّتني, with a shadda but no alif after the s. It is read here as sārratnī, from Form III sārra, “to speak secretly to someone”, with the missing long ā marked by a small dagger alif. The other possible reading, sarratnī, “she gladdened me”, does not fit the bad news that follows, but the reading remains a guess. After sārra, bi- marks the thing confided: mā … bihi, “what … of it”, where -hi points back to mā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ لَا وَاللَّهِ يَا سَيِّدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu lā wa-Allāhi yā sayyidī
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: No, by-God, O my-master.
sentences.i: “No, by God, my lord,” the jeweller replied.
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: the wāw of oath, followed by the genitive. The jeweller, a tradesman, gives ʿAlī the courteous sayyidī, “my master”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ إِنَّهَا زَعَمَتْ أَنِّي أَشَرْتُ عَلَى أَبِي الْحَسَنِ بِالْمَسِيرِ إِلَى الْبَصْرَةِ وَأَنَّنِي دَبَّرْتُ بِذَلِكَ حِيلَةً لِأَجْلِ عَدَمِ الْمُرَاسَلَةِ وَالْمُوَاصَلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla innahā zaʿamat annī ashartu ʿalā Abī al-Ḥasani bi-al-masīri ilā al-Baṣrati wa-annanī dabbartu bi-dhālika ḥīlatan li-ajli ʿadami al-murāsalati wa-al-muwāṣalati
sentences.l: And he-said: She claimed that I advised Abū al-Ḥasan to the going to Basra, and that I contrived by-that a-ruse for-the-sake-of (the) lack of the exchanging-of-letters and the keeping-in-touch.
sentences.i: “She claims,” he said, “that it was I who advised Abū al-Ḥasan to go away to Basra, and that I devised this as a ruse to put an end to the letters and the meetings.
sentences.n: zaʿama, “to claim, allege”, usually of a claim the speaker does not believe. ashāra ʿalā … bi-, “to advise someone to do something”: ʿalā marks the person advised, bi- the course advised. annī and annanī, “that I”, stand side by side; the second simply has an extra n. dabbartu bi-dhālika ḥīlatan, “I contrived a ruse by means of it”: bi- is instrumental. li-ajli ʿadami …, “for the sake of the absence of …”, that is, “so that there should be no more …”. al-murāsala, “exchanging letters”, and al-muwāṣala, “keeping in touch, meeting”, are both Form III verbal nouns, a matching pair that also rhyme.

sentences.t: فَحَلَفْتُ لَهَا أَنَّ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَكُنْ فَلَمْ تُصَدِّقْنِي وَمَضَتْ إِلَي سَيِّدَتِهَا وَهِيَ عَلَى مَا هِيَ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ سُوءِ الظَّنِّ لِأَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تَمِيلُ وَتُصْغِي إِلَى أَبِي الْحَسَنِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥalaftu lahā anna dhālika lam yakun fa-lam tuṣaddiqnī wa-maḍat ilā sayyidatihā wa-hiya ʿalā mā hiya ʿalayhi min sūʾi al-ẓanni li-annahā kānat tamīlu wa-tuṣghī ilā Abī al-Ḥasani
sentences.l: And I-swore to-her that that had-not been, and she-did-not believe-me, and went to her-mistress, she (being) upon what she (is) upon of evil-of-opinion, because she used-to incline and lend-ear to Abū al-Ḥasan.
sentences.i: I swore to her that it was not so, but she would not believe me, and she went back to her mistress as full of suspicion as ever, for she had always been fond of Abū al-Ḥasan and had listened to him.”
sentences.n: The ḍamma of فحلفتُ is the print's own. anna dhālika lam yakun, “that that had not been”: it never happened. fa-lam tuṣaddiqnī, “and she did not believe me”: the fa- has the force of “but”. The print writes ilā with a dotted yāʾ (الي). wa-hiya ʿalā mā hiya ʿalayhi, “she being upon what she is upon”, is a fixed phrase for “just as she was”. sūʾ al-ẓann, “evil of opinion”, means suspicion; the shadda of الظنّ is the print's own. kānat tamīlu, kāna with an imperfect, gives a habit in the past. The two verbs share one ilā: māla ilā, “to incline towards”, and aṣghā ilā, “to lend an ear to” (Form IV). The “she” is most naturally the slave-girl, who had trusted Abū al-Ḥasan as go-between and now blames the friend she thinks sent him away; it could also be read of her mistress.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشَّابُّ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ يَا أَخِي إِنِّي فَهِمْتُ مِنْ حَالِ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةِ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ وَاطَّلَعْتُ عَلَيْهِ وَلَكِنْ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى أَكُونُ عَوْنًا لَكَ عَلَى مُرَادِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shābbu al-jawhariyyu yā akhī innī fahimtu min ḥāli hādhihi al-jāriyati hādhā al-amra wa-iṭṭalaʿtu ʿalayhi wa-lākin in shāʾa Allāhu taʿālā akūnu ʿawnan laka ʿalā murādika
sentences.l: And the young-man the jeweller said: O my-brother, I understood from (the) state of this slave-girl this matter and became-acquainted with-it; but if God (the) Exalted wills, I-shall-be a-help to-you toward your-desire.
sentences.i: The young jeweller said, “My brother, I could see how things stood from this girl's manner, and I understood it all. But, God willing, I will help you to what you desire.”
sentences.n: al-shābb al-jawharī, “the young man, the jeweller”: the two nouns stand in apposition. iṭṭalaʿa ʿalā, “to learn of, be acquainted with”, is Form VIII of ṭalaʿa; the t of the form is swallowed by the root's ṭ, hence the doubled ṭṭ. wa-lākin barely contrasts here: “be that as it may”. in shāʾa Allāh stands as an aside, so akūnu stays in the plain indicative. ʿawnan laka ʿalā murādika, “a help to you towards your desire”: ʿalā marks the end you are helped towards. murād, “what is wished for”, is the passive participle of arāda.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ فَمَنْ لِي بِذَلِكَ وَكَيْفَ تَعْمَلُ مَعَهَا وَهِيَ تَنْفِرُ كَوَحْشِ الْفَلَاةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin fa-man lī bi-dhālika wa-kayfa taʿmalu maʿahā wa-hiya tanfiru ka-waḥshi al-falāti
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said to-him: So who (is) for-me with that? And how will-you-do with-her, when she shies like (the) wild-beasts of the desert?
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to him, “And who could bring that about for me? How will you manage her, when she shies away like a wild creature of the desert?”
sentences.n: man lī bi-dhālika, “who is there for me with that?”, is an idiom of longing, “who will get me that?”: li- marks the one in want, bi- the thing wanted. The fatḥa of فمَن is the print's own. taʿmalu maʿahā, “you do with her”, means deal with her. wa-hiya tanfiru, “when she shies”, is a circumstantial clause. nafara is the word for an animal that takes fright and bolts; waḥsh al-falāt, “the wild beasts of the open desert”, with ka-, “like”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ وَاللَّهِ لَابُدَّ أَنِّي أَبْذُلُ جُهْدِي فِي مُسَاعَدَتِكَ وَاحْتِيَالِي فِى التَّوَصُّلِ إِلَيْهَا مِنْ غَيْرِ كَشْفِ سِتْرٍ وَلَا مَضَرَّةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu wa-Allāhi lā budda annī abdhulu juhdī fī musāʿadatika wa-iḥtiyālī fī al-tawaṣṣuli ilayhā min ghayri kashfi sitrin wa-lā maḍarratin
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: By-God, there-is-no escape (from it) that I-expend my-effort in helping-you, and my-contriving in the reaching to-her, without uncovering of-a-veil or harm.
sentences.i: “By God,” he said, “I will spare no effort in helping you, and no cunning in finding a way to her, without anything being exposed and without harm to anyone.”
sentences.n: lā budda anna, “there is no escape from (the fact) that”: “I will surely”. The print runs lā budda together as one word (لابد); the spacing is kept. badhala juhdahu, “to spend one's effort”. iḥtiyālī, “my contriving”, a Form VIII verbal noun from the root of ḥīla, “ruse”, is a second object beside juhdī: “my effort in helping you, and my scheming in reaching her”. The print writes the second fī as فى. tawaṣṣul ilā, Form V, “to find a way to, gain access to”; its shadda is the print's own. kashf sitr, “the lifting of a veil”, is the exposure of what ought to stay hidden; maḍarra is “harm”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اسْتَأْذَنَهُ فِى الِانْصِرَافِ فَقَالَ لَهُ عَلِيُّ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ يَا أَخِي عَلَيْكَ بِكِتْمَانِ السِّرِّ
sentences.tr: thumma istaʾdhanahu fī al-inṣirāfi fa-qāla lahu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin yā akhī ʿalayka bi-kitmāni al-sirri
sentences.l: Then he-asked-his-leave for the departing; and ʿAlī son of Bakkār said to-him: O my-brother, upon-you (be) the keeping of the secret.
sentences.i: Then he asked leave to go, and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to him, “My brother, be sure you keep the secret.”
sentences.n: istaʾdhana, Form X of adhina, “to ask someone's leave”: the person is the object, and fī marks what leave is asked for. The hamza of استأذنه is the print's own. The print again writes ابن with its alif between the two names. ʿalayka bi-, “upon you is …”, is a set way of laying a duty on someone, “see that you …”: bi- marks what is enjoined. kitmān, “concealment”; the shadda of السرّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ وَبَكَى فَوَدَّعَهُ وَانْصَرَفَ
sentences.tr: thumma naẓara ilayhi wa-bakā fa-waddaʿahu wa-inṣarafa
sentences.l: Then he-looked at-him and wept; and he-bade-him-farewell and went-away.
sentences.i: Then ʿAlī looked at him and wept, and the jeweller bade him farewell and went away.
sentences.n: The verbs change subject without a name: it is most naturally ʿAlī who looks at his friend and weeps, and the jeweller who says goodbye and leaves.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept.
